paper_title: Meta Expert: Cross-Layer Expert Sharing for Storage- and Retrieval-Efficient MoE

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: As model parameters scale up, sparsely activated Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) approaches have become essential for model scaling. However, mainstream models currently adopt hierarchical architectures, where experts in different layers, although topologically independent, exhibit substantial similarity and redundancy in their stored content. Compared to the hierarchically arranged \textbf{Local Expert} in existing mainstream models, we hypothesize that inter-layer shared \textbf{Meta Expert} hold greater potential. To this end, we conduct a multi-dimensional empirical comparison between Local and Meta Experts, and find that models incorporating Meta Experts exhibit lower parameter redundancy, together with lower cross-entropy loss and higher downstream task accuracy. With the activated quantity and the expert granularity held fixed, \textbf{our model matches the performance of Vanilla MoE using only 70--80\% of the experts}, substantially improving the model's scaling potential. Beyond removing inter-layer redundancy among experts and improving information storage efficiency, our theoretical analysis further shows that, compared with Local Experts, Meta Experts provide hidden states with more flexible residual pathways, thereby improving information retrieval efficiency.

sections.title: ABSTRACT
sections.content: As model parameters scale up, sparsely activated Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) approaches have become essential for model scaling. However, mainstream models currently adopt hierarchical architectures, where experts in different layers, although topologically independent, exhibit substantial similarity and redundancy in their stored content. Compared to the hierarchically arranged Local Expert in existing mainstream models, we hypothesize that inter-layer shared Meta Expert hold greater potential. To this end, we conduct multi-dimensional empirical comparison between Local and Meta Experts, and find that models incorporating Meta Experts exhibit lower parameter redundancy, together with lower crossentropy loss and higher downstream task accuracy. With the activated quantity and the expert granularity held fixed, our model matches the performance of Vanilla MoE using only 7080% of the experts, substantially improving the models scaling potential. Beyond removing inter-layer redundancy among experts and improving information storage efficiency, our theoretical analysis further shows that, compared with Local Experts, Meta Experts provide hidden states with more flexible residual pathways, thereby improving information retrieval efficiency.

sections.title: INTRODUCTION
sections.content: Figure 1: Comparison between Vanilla and Meta-Expert models. All models are trained under the optimal setting of the Vanilla model, at varying depths and scales. Models with Meta Experts achieve comparable loss to the Vanilla baselines with only 7080% as many experts, or 7590% as many parameters, and the savings in both experts and parameters grow as the models get deeper and larger, indicating the favorable scalability of Meta Experts. In recent years, large language models (LLMs) have gradually approached or even surpassed humanlevel ability in general text, mathematics, and code (Brown et al., 2020; OpenAI et al., 2024). This progress owes much to the increasing scale of model parameters and training data: intelligence has been improved substantially as both factors grow (Kaplan et al., 2020; Hoffmann et al., 2022b). *Equal contribution. Corresponding author. 1 Preprint To enable ever-larger models, parameter sparsification has become an important approach (Shazeer et al., 2017; Fedus et al., 2022; Muennighoff et al., 2025). As the module that accounts for the vast majority of model parameters, the feed-forward network was originally densely computed block. (Vaswani et al., 2017a). However, as model size grows, such dense computation gradually becomes prohibitively expensive, creating efficiency bottlenecks for both training and inference (Lepikhin et al., 2021; Fedus et al., 2022). Meanwhile, although feed-forward networks are densely computed, only sparse subset of parameters is actually activated for given token during its forward pass (Li et al., 2023; Mirzadeh et al., 2024); the remaining inactive parameters still participate in the computation, leading to substantial waste. To address this, researchers have proposed designing feed-forward networks with natively sparseactivation structure, most notably the Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) (Shazeer et al., 2017; Fedus et al., 2022). MoE splits the feed-forward network into multiple sub-networks along the intermediate dimension and routes each token to only limited number of them before computation. This design endows the model with large total parameter count while ensuring that each tokens forward pass computation uses only small fraction of parameters, reconciling scale with efficiency. With the advent of increasingly sparse MoE models, parameter efficiency along the width dimension has been steadily improved (Dai et al., 2024). In this work, however, we ask how parameter efficiency can be improved along the depth dimension (Raposo et al., 2024). On the one hand, interpretability studies suggest that feed-forward networks store relatively static knowledge (Geva et al., 2021; Dai et al., 2022), and that different layers may store similar knowledge, suggesting nontrivial redundancy across layers (Meng et al., 2022; Takase & Kiyono, 2023; Fan et al., 2019; Chen et al., 2025; Men et al., 2025). On the other hand, Looped Transformers reuse the same parameters across recurrent applications of block (Dehghani et al., 2018; Giannou et al., 2023; Bai et al., 2019; Csordas et al., 2024; Chen et al., 2026a),and recent work shows that this design can attain the reasoning performance of much larger models with far fewer parameters (Bae et al., 2025; Saunshi et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2026). This benefit, however, comes with additional recursions and greater serial depth, incurring higher computational and latency costs. To balance parameter storage efficiency and computational cost, this work explores the potential of another Parameter Loop scheme Cross-Layer Expert Sharing. Unlike Looped Transformers, which keep the total parameters of each layer unchanged but increase the number of recursions, we aim to keep the number of recursions unchanged while increasing the candidate experts of each layer, and use the sparse activation of MoE to keep both the activated parameters and the computation per layer unchanged. We refer to the experts shared across layers as Meta Experts, and the layer-private experts in the conventional design as Local Experts. Our experiments show that, compared with the Local Expert of hierarchical architectures, Meta Experts reduce parameter redundancy and achieve lower cross-entropy loss together with higher downstream task accuracy. At fixed number of activated experts and expert granularity, our model achieves comparable performance to Vanilla MoE with only 70% as many experts, indicating substantially higher effective capacity per parameter. Further analysis reveals another reason why cross-layer expert sharing is effective: Meta Experts provide hidden states with more flexible paths for storage and retrieval. Compared with hierarchical architectures, cross-layer expert sharing implicitly provides more flexible residual connections: beyond the forward residual connections, it introduces backward residual connection at the activation levelone that operates within single forward pass and is therefore absent from existing models. Our contributions are summarized as follows: (1) systematic analysis of the effect of Meta Experts on model performance, covering their activation and total-number ratios among all experts, their presence in every layer, and their partial hierarchical organization. Although these configurations moderately affect performance, Meta Experts consistently bring significant improvements. (2) An explanation of why Meta Experts are effective from the perspective of residual connections. By comparing the forward hidden-state updates and the backward parameter updates of models with and without Meta Experts, we show that this design grants shallow and deep layers bidirectional access to representations across depth, enabling more flexible information retrieval. Preprint Figure 2: The Implementation of Local and Meta Experts. In contrast to the layer-private Local Experts, Meta Experts are shared across all layers.

sections.title: 3 EMPIRICAL COMPARISON BETWEEN META AND LOCAL EXPERTS
sections.content: To systematically analyze the effect of Meta Experts on model performance, we start from model with only Local Experts and incorporate Meta Experts in various forms, comparing model capabilities with and without them. 3.1 SETUPS Core Variables. We consider two types of relationship between Meta Experts and Local Experts: (1) the quantitative relationship: the ratio of their total numbers within the whole model and their activated numbers within each layer (See Fig 3.(a)); (2) the topological relationship: whether every layer contains both Meta and Local Experts (See Fig 3.(b)), and whether the Meta Experts are also hierarchically organized (See Fig 3.(c)). 3 Preprint Figure 3: The Quantitative and Topological Comparison between Meta and Local Experts. Common Settings. During the experiments, we first sweep all the variables on 2B-A0.5B model, and then select the relatively better-performing configurations for the scaling ladder experiments. Throughout the experiments, we keep the total number of experts and the total activation count fixed, which indirectly ensures that different models have similar FLOPs, enabling fairer comparison. When comparing models at different FLOPs, all models adopt the training-optimal configuration of the Vanilla MoE structure, rather than configuration tuned specifically for our design. Detailed experimental setups can be found in A.3 Metrics. In addition to cross-entropy loss and downstream task accuracy, we introduce an expertredundancy metric as complementary perspective for analyzing expert specialization under different architectural settings. It allows us to examine how expert topology affects the overlap among learned expert functions. The exact training configurations and the definition of the redundancy metric are deferred to Appendix A.2. 3.2 META/LOCAL EXPERTS RATIO We first study the effect of the ratio between the total numbers of Meta Experts and Local Experts, and of their activation ratio within each layer, on model performance. Settings. For the total-number ratio, we consider Meta Expert proportions of 0%, 25%, 50%, 75%, or 100%; for the activation ratio, we consider proportions of 25%, 50%, or 75%. For concreteness, consider two-layer model with 256 experts in total and 8 experts activated per layer. Meta/Local number ratio of 75% then corresponds to 192 Meta Experts, shared across all layers, and 32 Local Experts per layer; an activation ratio of 75% corresponds to activating 6 Meta Experts and 2 Local Experts per layer. Figure 4: Pilot experiments on the Meta/Local Expert ratio. We vary the total-number proportion of Meta Experts (0%100%) and their per-layer activation proportion (25%75%), while keeping the total expert count and the total activation count fixed so that all models share similar FLOPs. Higher Meta-Expert proportions consistently reduce both the cross-entropy loss and the expert redundancy ρ; increasing the activation share of Local Experts reduces redundancy but degrades the loss. 4 Preprint Pilot Experiments (Fig 4). The results show that, at any activation ratio, higher total-parameter proportion of Meta Experts consistently leads to lower loss and redundancy; meanwhile, allocating higher activation ratio to Meta Experts also helps reduce the loss. Taken together, these observations attest to the effectiveness of Meta Experts. On the other hand, while assigning higher activation ratio to Local Experts is detrimental to the loss, it does help reduce the redundancy among experts. This suggests that, compared with Meta Experts, Local Expertseach of which is activated in only one layer under the traditional architecturemay be harder to train sufficiently, and this undertraining may give rise to redundancy. Figure 5: Scaling-ladder on the Meta/Local Expert ratio. With the per-layer activation fixed to 4 Meta Experts and 4 Local Experts, we scale the total-number ratio of Meta Experts (25%/50%/75%) across training compute (FLOPs). Although slightly worse than Pure-Meta-Expert Setting, the 75% ratio achieves the best cross-entropy loss over all Partial-Meta Experts setting at every compute budget, and is adopted as the base configuration in all subsequent experiments. Scaling Ladder (Fig 5). Given that activating 4 Meta Experts and 4 Local Experts per layer yields consistently better loss, we hold this activation ratio fixed and conduct full scaling-ladder validation across the total-number ratios of 25%/50%/75%. The results confirm that, although still slightly worse than the Pure-Meta-Expert setting, the 75% ratio achieves the best performance over all Partial-Meta settings at every compute budget, in terms of both cross-entropy loss and expert redundancy. Considering that model with only Meta Experts may suffer from training instability, we adopt the 75% configuration in all subsequent experiments. 3.3 META/LOCAL EXPERTS TOPOLOGY We next investigate the effect of the topology of Meta/Local Experts on model performance. On the one hand, we explore whether every layer should include Meta Experts; on the other hand, we explore whether the Meta Experts should themselves be partially hierarchically organized. Settings. On the one hand, we consider variants in which Local Experts are used exclusively, with no Meta Experts introduced at all: either in only the first 1, 2, 4, or 8 layers of the model, in only the last 1, 2, 4, or 8 layers, or in both the first and the last 1, 2, or 4 layers. On the other hand, we consider partitioning the Meta Experts into 2, 4, or 8 sub-pools, which are then accessed in looped mannereither in chunked or an interleaved fashion. Pilot Experiments (Fig 6). It can be observed that both operationsintroducing Local-Expertsonly layers, and organizing the Meta Experts hierarchically so as to mimic the topology of Local Expertsgenerally incur loss degradation, which further demonstrates the positive role of Meta Experts in model performance. Notably, under lighter degree of intervention, the loss slightly improves: for example, when only the first two and the last two layers are restricted to Local Experts, or when the Meta Experts are looped only twice. This suggests, on the one hand, that experts in the shallowest and deepest layers serve more differentiated functions, with essentially no mutual redundancy between these layersa conclusion also supported by the expert redundancy measurements. On the other hand, mildly hierarchical Meta Experts help improve the model capability slightly; hierarchy, however, introduces certain amount of expert redundancy, and why this redundancy does not translate into higher loss remains an open question for further investigation. Scaling Ladder (Fig 7). Compared with other configurations, introducing Local-Experts-only layers at both the shallow and the deep ends, and partitioning the Meta Experts into sub-pools in an 5 Preprint Figure 6: Pilot experiments on the Meta/Local Expert topology. We vary where Local Experts are used exclusively (the first and/or the last 1/2/4/8 layers), and how the Meta Experts are hierarchically organized (2/4/8 sub-pools, accessed in looped manner, either chunked or interleaved). Both interventions generally degrade the loss, corroborating the benefit of Meta Experts, while lighter degree of interventiononly the first and the last two layers restricted to Local Experts, or the Meta Experts looped only twiceslightly improves it. interleaved manner, yield consistently better results; we therefore supplement full scaling-ladder validation under these two configurations. The results show that, at every FLOPs configuration, the best performance is achieved by using Local Experts exclusively in the first two and the last two layers, together with partitioning the Meta Experts into 2 sub-pools. We also observe that, as the model becomes deeper, using more Local-Experts-only layers and larger hierarchy of Meta Experts likewise exhibits better results. This suggests, on the one hand, that the proportion of specialized shallow and deep layers relative to the total number of layers may remain roughly constant as model depth changes; on the other hand, deeper models also call for larger hierarchical expert topology; the Local Experts of the Vanilla model, however, are overly hierarchical, and can therefore only achieve suboptimal results. Overall Comparison (Fig 1 & 8) We combine the best configurations identified in each ablation and find that the combined model consistently outperforms every individual configuration in terms of loss. Building on this best configuration, we further reduce the number of Meta Experts and find that, compared with the Vanilla model, models with Meta Experts save approximately 2030% of the experts (or 1525% of the parameters, since other modules also account for certain fraction of the parameters), with the advantage becoming more pronounced as the model size grows. 3.4 DOWNSTREAM PERFORMANCE OF META EXPERTS-BASED MODEL For more comprehensive comparison, beyond cross-entropy loss, we further compare the downstream task capabilities of different configurations through training at larger scale. Settings. Using the best configuration identified in each of the ablation studies above, we train 6BA1.6B models for 200B tokens and evaluate their downstream task performance. We compare five variants: the Vanilla baseline (Vanilla MoE, Local Experts only), the MR75 model, which activates Meta Experts at 75% meta ratio, and three topological refinements of MR75MR75 + Loop2, which partitions the Meta Experts into two interleaved sub-pools; MR75 + F2L2, which restricts the first two and last two layers to Local Experts only; and their combination, MR75 + F2L2 + Loop2. All variants use the same total number of experts, per-layer activation budget, and training recipe, 6 Preprint Figure 7: Scaling-ladder on the Meta/Local Expert topology. We scale the two best pilot configurationsLocal Experts exclusively at both shallow and deep ends, and interleaved sub-pool partitioning of the Meta Expertsacross training compute (FLOPs). Restricting the first two and the last two layers to Local Experts, together with 2 sub-pools, achieves the best performance at every compute budget; as the model becomes deeper, more Local-Experts-only layers and larger hierarchy of Meta Experts further help, suggesting that deeper models call for larger hierarchical expert topology. Figure 8: Scaling-ladder on cumulative Meta-Expert designs. Starting from 75% Meta-Expert total-number ratio (MR75), we incrementally add topology refinementsLocal Experts only in the first and last two layers (F2L2) and two looped Meta-Expert sub-pools (Loop2)and finally combine both (F2L2 + Loop2). All models are compared against the Vanilla MoE (dashed line at 1.0) in loss ratio L/LVanilla (left) and expert redundancy ratio R/RVanilla (right) across training compute (FLOPs). Every refinement improves over Vanilla at every compute budget, with the largest gains under the combined design; the advantage in both loss and redundancy becomes more pronounced as training compute grows. ensuring that performance differences are attributable to the expert topology. We evaluate the models across diverse set of benchmarks covering complementary capabilities: world knowledge and factual question answering in both English (MMLU (Hendrycks et al., 2021)) and Chinese (CEval (Huang et al., 2023) and CMMLU (Li et al., 2024)); multi-step and commonsense reasoning (BBH (Kazemi et al., 2025) with chain-of-thought and OpenBookQA (Mihaylov et al., 2018)); and open-ended, knowledge-intensive generation (TriviaQA (Joshi et al., 2017)). Results. Table 1 reports the downstream performance of the five expert-topology variants after training on 200B tokens. Due to the limited training budget, different Meta Expert variants exhibit advantages across different datasets, highlighting the need for larger-scale scaling experiments, but incorporating Meta Experts consistently outperform the vanilla baseline. 7 Preprint Table 1: Downstream results for the 6B-A1.6B models after training on 200B tokens. MMLU / C-Eval / CMMLU are 5-shot accuracy, OpenBookQA is normalized accuracy, and BBH / TriviaQA are generation exact-match. The best result per dataset is in bold. Vanilla is the Local-Experts-only baseline (Vanilla MoE); MR75 activates Meta Experts at 75% meta ratio; + Loop2 partitions the Meta Experts into two interleaved sub-pools; and + F2L2 restricts the first two and last two layers to Local Experts only. sections.title: 5 CONCLUSION
sections.content: In this work, we present an empirical and theoretical analysis of cross-layer expert sharing in MoE models, contrasting the hierarchically arranged Local Experts of standard architectures with interlayer shared Meta Experts. Our systematic comparisonsover the Meta/Local ratio, the activation ratio, and the topology of the shared poolshow that Meta Experts consistently reduce expert redundancy and cross-entropy loss while improving downstream task accuracy: at fixed number of activated experts and expert granularity, models built on shared experts match the performance of Vanilla MoE with only 7080% of the expert budget, substantially improving scaling potential. Beyond these empirical observations, our analysis shows that shared expert block is not merely parameter-saving device: it widens the forward residual connections and grants hidden states bidirectional access to expert content across depth, improving both the storage and the retrieval of 9 (7) (8) Preprint information. Taken together, our results suggest that inter-layer redundancy, long treated as an intrinsic cost of deep MoE models, can instead be converted into effective capacity. Future directions include extending this analysis to larger models and broader architectures, and understanding why mildly hierarchical shared experts introduce redundancy without degrading performance. AI USE STATEMENT In this work, we used generative AI tools for writing assistance: polishing language and grammar, brainstorming alternative phrasings (e.g., for the paper title and section openings), formalizing the presentation of the theoretical analysis (e.g., LATEX derivations whose underlying ideas are the authors own), and drafting descriptive passages (figure captions, the Related Work section, and the Conclusion) based on author-provided outlines, notes, and experimental results. We also used generative AI tools for code assistance, including implementation support and plotting scripts for the result figures; all designs, algorithms, and experimental ideas were proposed by the authors. We have not used generative AI tools for research ideation, experimental design. We have reviewed all AI-assisted work: all AI-drafted text was checked, revised, and approved by the authors; translations were verified against the authors intended meaning; all technical claims, equations, and reported numbers were independently verified by the authors against their own derivations and experimental results; and AI-generated code was verified, tested, and debugged by the authors for correctness, with all result figures manually checked against the underlying data. We take responsibility for the final content of this work, including text, claims or artifacts produced with the aid of generative AI. REPRODUCIBILITY STATEMENT We have taken several steps to make the results in this paper reproducible, and we reference here the parts of the paper that support them. The complete experimental configuration for the scaling ladder is given in Appendix A.3: the per-depth architecture is listed in Table 2 and the per-depth training scheduleglobal batch size, optimizer steps, warmup and decay, learning rate, token budget, and training FLOPsin Table 3. Every rung, and every architectural variant at given rung, shares the same backbone, optimizer, and parallelism policy; only the depth-dependent knobs in those tables change, so single set of hyperparameters fully specifies each run. The evaluation protocol used for the compute-versus-loss analysis is described in the same appendix: for each run we report the language-modeling loss averaged over the final ten training steps. Our models are implemented on top of Megatron-LM, widely used open-source framework, which helps ensure reproducibility.

sections.title: A APPENDIX
sections.content: A.1 RELATED WORK Weight Tying was originally introduced to share parameters between the embedding layer and the language model head (Press & Wolf, 2017; Inan et al., 2016): since the two matrices map tokens to and from the hidden space, tying them nearly halves the corresponding parameters while often improving perplexity, and the practice has become standard in modern language models (Vaswani et al., 2017b; Raffel et al., 2020). Beyond tying modules at the same depth, weight tying can be pushed further, to reusing parameters across depth (Dehghani et al., 2018; Lan et al., 2019). Looped Transformer pushes weight tying to extreme: the same block is applied multiple times per token, unrolling small set of weights into arbitrary depth (Dehghani et al., 2018; Giannou et al., 15 Preprint 2023; Hua et al., 2025). This line of work shows that weight reuse across depth can substitute for parameter growth, and that compact recurrent model can match the reasoning performance of much larger ones (Bae et al., 2025; Saunshi et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2026), at the cost of additional recursions and higher degree of serialization. Meta Experts share the same motivationextracting more effective capacity from fixed parameter budgetbut apply tying at finer granularity and within single feed-forward pass: only the expert block is reused across layers, without extra recursions, so training and inference retain the parallelism of standard Transformers, while attention may remain layer-specific. Depending on what is reused across depth, this paradigm subsumes several lines of work. Attn Weight Sharing reuses the attention projections (or entire attention blocks) of different layers, yielding moderate parameter savings at little accuracy cost (Xiao et al., 2019; Lan et al., 2019; Mu et al., 2026). These results suggest that the per-layer parameter budget of Transformers is partially redundantbut leave open where the redundancy concentrates and whether the same principle applies to the rest of the block. Attn KV-Cache Sharing reuses not parameters but activations: in long-context or serving scenarios, multiple layers attend to common KV cache, trading representational independence for inference memory and throughput (Sun et al., 2024; Brandon et al., 2024; Zuhri et al., 2025; Wu & Tu, 2024; Wu et al., 2025). Such sharing is typically applied at deployment time, affects the cache rather than the learned weights, and is often found to be nearly lossless suggesting that layers can tolerate reading the same content, but not that they should store the same content. Meta Experts operate on the storage side: the shared expert pool is written by every layer during training, so cross-layer sharing reshapes what the model stores and how hidden states retrieve it, rather than merely reusing cached activations at inference. FFN Weight Sharing is the closest line to our work: it reuses feed-forward parameters across layers, either by tying the FFN of all layers or by sharing it among subset (Lan et al., 2019; Pires et al., 2023; Thawakar et al., 2024). Existing studies, however, focus on dense FFNs and report mixed results, and sharing is typically applied uniformly to every layer. MoE Weight Sharing has been explored in several recent works: experts are shared across layers, but almost always under an everylayer sharing topology, whose communication and memory overhead is difficult to scale (Li et al., 2025; Tan et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2026a; Huang et al., 2026; Chen et al., 2026b; Jiao et al., 2026). Meta Experts generalize this idea to more flexible regime: shared pool of experts is accessed through several topology that is more friendly for communication and memory (reserving boundary layers for local experts, sub-pool partitioning with chunked or interleaved access), allows the model to decide which content is worth sharing across depthand, as our analysis shows, implicitly turns the shared experts into bidirectional residual pathways between layers. A.2 REDUNDANCY METRIC To quantify how much of models expert capacity is redundant, we need measure that is (i) continuous, with no similarity threshold; (ii) comparable across architectures with different expert counts and depths; and (iii) faithful to the correlation structure among experts in high dimensions, where naive cosine similarities collapse toward zero. Our metric is built from single similarity kernel and single spectral statistic. Similarity kernel: linear-CKA on centered covariances. For expert i, let Yi RT be its response matrix to shared probe set of L2-normalized tokens, and let denote Yi with its sample mean subtracted. We map each expert to the vectorized centered covariance and define the pairwise similarity as the cosine in this feature space, ϕi = vec(cid:0)Y Y (cid:1), Kij = ϕi, ϕj ϕi ϕj , (9) (10) which is exactly linear CKA evaluated on the experts functional responses. Being invariant to orthogonal transformations and isotropic scaling, Kij reflects the correlated directions between experts rather than their absolute orientation or norm, and avoids the collapse of raw high-dimensional cosine. The resulting Gram matrix REE covers the experts under analysis: for models mixing Meta and Local Experts the two pools are concatenated on the expert axis and analyzed jointly, and for layer-wise models the layer index serves as the grouping axis. 16 Preprint Spectral statistic: how many directions collapse. Since is positive semi-definite, its eigenspectrum λ1 λ2 λE 0 distributes the total similarity energy across principal directions. We measure the concentration of this energy by the Gini coefficient of the spectrum, (cid:80) ρ = Gini(λ) = [0, 1], (11) i,j λi λj 2E (cid:80) λi where ρ = 0 means the energy is uniform across all directions (experts fully complementary, no redundancy) and ρ 1 means it concentrates on few directions (strong redundancy). The reading admits an exact interpretation: for uniform rank-k spectrum, Gini(λ) = 1 k/E, so ρ equals the fraction of expert directions that have collapsed into redundant ones. Because ρ is ratio, it is directly comparable across models with different E, depths, and training budgets, and we report it as our headline Expert Redundancy metric. A.3 SCALING-LADDER EXPERIMENTAL SETTINGS Models and training. All models are trained from scratch on NVIDIA H200 GPUs. The scaling experiments use single family of Qwen3.5-style, text-only Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models arranged as depth-controlled ladder at four depths {12, 16, 20, 24}; model width is scaled jointly with depth so that each rung is (approximately) compute-optimal, giving clean computeversus-loss axis. At each rung, the vanilla baseline and every Meta Experts variant are trained independently, sharing the same backbone architecture and training configuration but no trained weights, and preserving the same 128 routed-expert budget, so only the depth-dependent knobs (width, batch size, learning rate, token budget, and expert parallelism) change across rungs (Tables 2 and 3). Table 2: Per-depth architecture of the scaling ladder. Every rung uses 128 routed experts plus one gated shared expert, top-8 routing, period-4 GDN/full-attention pattern (one quarter full attention), and head dimension of 256. Widths scale jointly with depth. The table specifies the shared vanilla backbone at each rung; the Meta Experts variants replace only the routed-expert layers and keep the same 128 routed-expert budget, so every variant at given rung shares these dimensions. GDN key/value entries are head counts (each head has dimension 128). Every transformer block carries an MoE feed-forward layer with 128 routed experts and one gated shared expert, whose intermediate widths scale with model width, and the router selects the top-8 experts per token with pre-softmax gating. We optimize with Muon (extra scale factor 0.2) under warmupstabledecay (WSD) schedule with an inverse-square-root decay shape: the peak learning rate decreases with depth (from 1.97 103 at L=12 to 1.278 103 at L=24), the minimum is one tenth of the peak, warmup spans tens of steps, and the decay phase spans the final 10% of training; all models use micro-batch size of 2 and sequence length of 8192. The reported loss is the training language-modeling loss averaged over the final ten steps, so all rungs are compared on the same quantity, and the per-rung token budget is GBS 8192 iters  (Table 3)  . Preprint All rungs use tensor-, pipeline-, and context-parallel size 1, scaling by data and expert parallelism only: the two smaller rungs (L {12, 16}) use expert-parallel size 1 with the all-gather token dispatcher, and the two larger rungs (L {20, 24}) use expert-parallel size 8, the all-to-all dispatcher, and block activation recomputation on the last 4 layers, with grouped GEMM and permute fusion enabled throughout. As an illustrative parameter scale, the L=16 vanilla backbone has 1.96B total parameters and 449M activated parameters per token. We do not tune the training hyperparameters per architectural variant. Instead we fix single compute-optimal configuration for the vanilla baseline backbone at each rung and reuse it unchanged for every Meta Experts variant. The baseline configurationthe joint depthwidth scaling, and the per-depth global batch size, peak learning rate, and token budget is obtained by sweeping these settings and retaining the compute-optimal choice at each depth, following established practice on compute-optimal training and its schedule (Hoffmann et al., 2022a; Hagele et al., 2024) and on scaling laws for the learning rate and batch size (Bi et al., 2024; Team et al., 2025). The Mixture-of-Experts structural choices (expert count, granularity, and the sharedexpert ratio) are likewise set in line with recent MoE scaling-law analyses (Tian et al., 2026; Zhao et al., 2025). Because every Meta Experts variant inherits the baseline configuration without retuning, difference in loss at rung reflects the architectural change rather than difference in hyperparameters; this reuse is further supported by evidence that optimal learning rate and batch size are governed primarily by the compute budget and are largely insensitive to Mixture-of-Experts architectural variation (Team et al., 2025). Moreover, at given depth every variant keeps the pertoken top-8 routing and hence the same activated parameters, and shares the same token budget, so all variants at rung incur the same training FLOPs and are plotted at single shared compute coordinate; the compute-versus-loss comparison at that rung is thus iso-FLOP by construction, and the only free axis across variants is the loss.
